messages.subject: minshade vs minshades clarification
parts:
Hello, 

Apologies if this has already been addressed, and I missed it. My colleague and I are in the early stages of developing our model and are having trouble figuring out the explicit difference between minshade and minshades and how they're applied in the context of the ectotherm model. 

Additionally, we are wondering what shade value is used in the ectotherm model if all behavioral parameters are set to 0 (e.g. a non-thermoregulating ectotherm). We have two environments of very different min and max shade values (which are set in the inputs) but have outputs that look identical. We are struggling to identify the disconnect. 

Any help understanding these details would be greatly appreciated. 

Thank you.

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: minshade vs minshades clarification
parts:
Hi Sidney,

Good questions. Originally you could only set a single value for minshade and maxshade for both the microclimate model and the ectotherm model. I subsequently added the facility of including time-varying shade (on a daily basis, e.g. to capture changes in vegetation structure) but kept the original input parameters for fixed shade, and just had the code create a vector of daily values on the fly if the user wasn't specifying time-varying shade. Your comment made me realise that this is a bit confusing. So,  I've made the following changes (now pushed to github):

1. For the microclimate model functions (e.g. micro_global, micro_usa, etc.), 'minshade' and 'maxshade' can be single values (constant through time) or a vector of daily values (which you can make variable through time, e.g. to simulate a fire). If you put single values, the code will internally convert them into a vector of daily values and the outputs 'minshade' and 'maxshade' from the function will be the vector of daily values.

2. For the ectotherm model, the 'minshade' input parameter is now gone, and it just has 'minshades' and 'maxshades' which, by default, are taken from the microclimate output list on the assumption that you've called this list 'micro', i.e. 'micro$minshade' and 'micro$maxshade'. But, you can override these if you wish with a different vector of shade values. This could be because, for example, you've simulated the microclimate of a forest floor where shade might be 90%, but you want to simulate an animal tracking a sun spot. Or, you might have simulated an animal in an unshaded microclimate but you want to simulate it sitting in the shade of a small object in that environment. So, in the first case the microclimate in terms of air temperature, ground temperature, sky temperature, humidity and wind speed is that of a forest floor, but the animal is receiving full sun from the sun spot. And vice versa for the second case.

Note also that the solar radiation returned by the microclimate model in 'metout' and 'shadmet' (column 'SOLR') is unshaded - this is so that the ectotherm model has the unshaded values available to it so you can run simulations of the type I just described, e.g. the sun spot example of experiencing 0% shade in a microclimate that is 90% shaded. I've now added a message to this effect in the microclimate functions. The thing to be mindful of here, though, is that the air temperature, sky temperature and ground temperature get adjusted by a weighting relating to the current shade value compared to the maximum one. E.g.

       TA = TA_MINSHADE*((MAXSHD-SHADE)/MAXSHD) +  TA_MAXSHADE *(SHADE/MAXSHD)

with MAXSHADE being the value for the day that you inputted via the 'maxshades' vector and SHADE being the value the model is currently using via the behavioural thermoregulation algorithm in the ectotherm model. I know all this is a bit complex, but so are microclimates and animals behaving in them :).

To answer your second question, if you set the simulation up so the animal can't thermoregulate, it will use the minimum shade microclimate. So if you want to simulate a non-thermoregulating animal under different shade levels, you want to vary 'minshade' in the microclimate model. Note also that there is the parameter 'live' which you can set to zero and the animal will be stuck on the surface in the minimum shade environment. Note that this setting turns of any metabolic heat generation (usually trivial for an ectotherm) or respiratory water loss, but cutaneous water loss still occurs.

If you're still not getting the outputs you expect from your simulations of different shade levels, post the code here and I'll take a look.

All the best,
Mike
